videos.title: D-Day’s First Battle | The British Airborne’s Fight for Pegasus Bridge
videos.desc: The Battle for Pegasus Bridge, D-Day, 6 June 1944. At sixteen minutes past midnight, six Horsa gliders came down in silence beside two bridges east of Sword Beach - the Caen Canal crossing at Bénouville and the swing bridge over the River Orne at Ranville. The 181 men of D Company, 2nd Ox and Bucks Light Infantry, under Major John Howard had one job: take both bridges intact before the Germans could blow them, and hold until relieved. videos.title: The Battle of Juno Beach D-Day 1944 | Canada's Longest Day (Animated)
videos.desc:
The Battle of Juno Beach, D-Day, 6 June 1944. At dawn on D-Day, the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division stormed Juno Beach — eight kilometres of Normandy seafront between the British beaches at Gold and Sword, where three quiet resort towns had been turned into fortresses. Courseulles-sur-Mer, Bernières-sur-Mer and Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer hid German guns in four feet of concrete, sighted along the sand, untouched by the naval bombardment. The Canadian objective on D-Day: take the three towns, push ten miles inland, and cut the road between Caen and Bayeux before nightfall.

videos.desc:
The Battle of Saint-Lô, July 1944. Six weeks after D-Day, the Allied advance through Normandy had stalled in the bocage - hedgerow country where every field was a fortress and every advance was paid for by the yard. To break out of Normandy, the American First Army needed Saint-Lô, the road junction of lower Normandy and the springboard for Operation Cobra.

videos.desc:

videos.title: Rangers Lead the Way: The D-Day Assault on Pointe du Hoc and Omaha Beach | Animated Documentary
videos.desc:
On June 6, 1944, Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder led 225 Rangers up the cliffs of Pointe du Hoc — scaling rope ladders under fire to destroy six heavy guns threatening both American invasion beaches. When they reached the top, the casemates were empty.

This is the full story of the U.S. Army Rangers on D-Day: the cliff assault at Pointe du Hoc, the desperate fighting on Omaha Beach, and the 48-hour battle to hold what they had taken — outnumbered, cut off, and waiting for a relief that came almost too late.
